analysis.one_liner: Toughens Medicare rules against hospitals dumping emergency patients, with penalties and patient lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committees without a single vote, after being referred in February 1989 and abandoned by that November.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill strengthened existing Medicare rules that stop hospitals from transferring emergency patients — often uninsured ones — before they are stabilized. It would have required hospitals to screen anyone who walks into the emergency department using the whole hospital's resources, get written informed consent before transferring or refusing treatment, send complete medical records with any transfer, post signs listing patients' rights, and accept appropriate transfers at hospitals with special capabilities like burn or trauma units. It barred hospitals from delaying care while checking a patient's insurance status, let patients sue for at least $25,000 per violation, and fined physicians up to $50,000 for falsifying records or pressuring patients into transfers.
analysis.who_benefits: Emergency patients — especially uninsured people, Medicare beneficiaries, and pregnant women — who would gain enforceable rights to a screening exam, stabilized treatment, and protection from being shipped to other hospitals for financial reasons. Patients would be able to sue hospitals and physicians directly, with attorney's fees available.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a medical screening exam using the whole hospital's capability, not just whatever the emergency department happens to have [S2][S3].
Bars hospitals from delaying a screening exam or treatment to ask about the patient's insurance or method of payment [S2][S3].

Prohibits transferring a patient with an unstabilized emergency condition unless the patient gives written informed consent, and requires all available medical records to travel with the transfer [S2][S3].
Lets patients sue hospitals or physicians for at least $25,000 per violation, with equitable relief and attorney's fees, and makes hospitals liable for their agents' and physicians' acts [S2][S3].

Fines physicians up to $50,000 and excludes them from Medicare for falsifying exam results, making false transfer certifications, or misrepresenting a patient's condition to force a transfer [S2][S3].

Requires hospitals with specialized capabilities such as burn units, shock-trauma units, and neonatal intensive care to accept appropriate transfers, and expands 'active labor' protections to any point in pregnancy where a transfer could threaten the mother or unborn child [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals — particularly those that had used transfers to move uninsured and unprofitable patients out of their emergency departments — would bear new liability, a $25,000 minimum damages floor in patient lawsuits, record-keeping duties, and mandatory acceptance of specialty transfers. Physicians responsible for emergency care would face civil money penalties up to $50,000 per violation and possible exclusion from Medicare.

drawbacks.text: The liability provisions — hospital responsibility for its physicians' acts, a $25,000 minimum damage award, and attorney's fees — would increase hospitals' legal exposure and could push up the cost of emergency care and encourage defensive medicine [S2][S3].

Requiring hospitals with specialized facilities to accept appropriate transfers shifts patient burdens onto regional referral centers, burn units, and neonatal intensive care units, which could strain their capacity [S3].
The compliance burden — five-year transfer memoranda, posted signage, and detailed informed-consent documentation — falls heaviest on smaller hospitals with thinner administrative staff [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are substantial and directly aimed at a real harm: hospitals turning away or transferring emergency patients who cannot pay. The main cost is higher liability and administrative burden on hospitals, and some of that cost is the point — it is the enforcement mechanism. The $25,000 minimum award and broad hospital liability for physicians are aggressive, and a fair critic could argue they overshoot; but the core screening, consent, and anti-delay rules are hard to argue against for patients.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and their health subcommittees for most of 1989, was never reported out for a House vote, and the record closes in November 1989 pointing to H.R. 3299.

narrative.text: Pete Stark introduced the bill on February 2, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees the same day [S1][S5].

In early February the bill went to the Subcommittee on Health in Ways and Means and the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment in Energy and Commerce, where it remained without further committee action [S5].
On November 22, 1989, the action history notes only 'See H.R. 3299', and the bill never received a floor vote in either chamber [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and physicians who preferred the looser existing transfer rules came out ahead: no new penalties, no minimum patient damages, and no duty to accept specialty transfers took effect through this bill.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: Chairman of the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 821 to tighten emergency transfer and patient-dumping rules under Medicare [S1][S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on February 7, 1989, and never reported it to the full House [S5].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee on February 13, 1989, and took no further action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with a single Republican cosponsor and died in committee without any roll-call vote, so no partisan pattern appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have ended the practice of transferring unstabilized emergency patients, required hospitals with specialty units to accept transfers, and exposed hospitals to $25,000-minimum lawsuits and five-year record-keeping. Hospitals that relied on moving uninsured patients out of their emergency departments bore the full cost of the new rules.

Physicians responsible for emergency exams and transfers would face civil money penalties up to $50,000 per violation and exclusion from Medicare for falsifying results or pressuring patients into transfers.

industries.industry: Specialty referral centers (burn, shock-trauma, and neonatal intensive care units)
industries.note: These facilities would be barred from refusing appropriate transfers of patients needing their specialized capabilities, taking on patient volume they could previously decline.
